evidence: The diff hunk confirms DOCS_FILE is the only classification pattern without /i, so a lowercase 'readme' fell to source; but the reviewer's minimal fix (add /i) applied to the greedy trailing [^/]*$ would newly capture 'licensed_users.csv' and 'readme_generator.js' as docs, the under-review direction, so the agent's simultaneous boundary tightening to (?:\.(?:md|...|txt))?$ was necessary, not extra.
guidance_note: When adding a flag to one member of a regex family, re-derive that pattern's accept/reject set under the new flag before shipping it - a flag that widens matching can turn a latent anchoring bug into a live misclassification.

evidence: DOCS_EXT genuinely listed .txt, so requirements.txt/constraints.txt classified as docs and a dependency-only PR would report kinds.source===0; the agent removed txt from DOCS_EXT and kept README.txt covered via the keyword pattern, which preserves the one legitimate .txt doc case the reviewer itself named.
guidance_note: When an extension list drives a lower-scrutiny classification, check each extension against the non-prose files that commonly carry it before adding it.

evidence: RegExp.test(undefined) does coerce to the string 'undefined', which matches none of the five patterns and returns 'source', so a fileless entry silently inflated kinds.source; the agent's loud throw is the right shape and its distinction from a defensive skip is sound - a skip would drop the entry with no signal.
guidance_note: State a total classifier's input contract at the top of the function and enforce it there, rather than relying on the pattern set to reject malformed input.

evidence: The guard added by 1127057 for F3 tested only `typeof filename !== 'string'`, so classifyFile('') still fell through every pattern to 'source' - the exact phantom-file failure the guard's own comment claimed to close, one round later.
guidance_note: When writing a contract guard against an absent value, reject every degenerate value the type admits (null, undefined, '') in that one guard, not only the wrong-type case.

evidence: The 1127057 diff shows this commit inserted tests above the churn assertion but never touched it, so the post-review-commit flag is a line-renumbering false positive on original PR code. The magic number is a real readability point, but the reviewer's premise that 4 encodes diffChurn internals is wrong - it is countable from the two fixture patches - and deleting it as proposed would have left only `churn === diffChurn(files)`, which is vacuous because assessDifficulty returns exactly diffChurn(files).
guidance_note: Name a fixture-derived expected value as a constant with the derivation in a comment when you write it, so it reads as ground truth rather than as a magic number a reviewer will ask you to delete.

evidence: `gh pr view 90 --json files` lists only package.json, package-lock.json, src/difficulty.js and test/difficulty.test.js - no dist/ - confirming the agent's claim that the bundle consumers execute was unchanged, and the repo's CONTRIBUTING.md states the rule as 'Pick the level by what the change does to the consumer contract, not by whether it is a fix or a feature', which defeats the reviewer's generic new-exports-means-minor premise. The [LAW:single-enforcer] citation is decorative: that law is about one enforcement checkpoint for a cross-cutting invariant in code, not about which versioning convention wins. The post-review-commit flag is a false positive - 1127057 did not touch package.json.

narrative: A small pure-module PR that took three rounds over five advisory findings and one pushback. The agent handled the two classification findings well, twice improving on the reviewer's proposed fix in ways that avoided introducing a bug (F1's greedy boundary, F5's vacuous assertion). The one genuine chain is F3 to F4: the input guard shipped rejecting non-strings but not the empty string, so the same silent-misclassification class came back a round later. Round 1's other two findings were on untouched original code that the flag mislabels as fix-caused.
guidance_observations: Both post-review rounds here were triggered by the reviewer re-reading the whole file each round, so relocated original lines get flagged as new - the flags in this packet are three-quarters false positives.

The agent twice declined the reviewer's literal fix and shipped a better one; in both cases the reviewer's fix would have made the code worse, which is evidence that address-pr-reviews' different_fix path is earning its keep.

evidence: The diff shows the PR replaced `budgetDeRated = dailyBudget > 0 && effort.roundCap !== defaultEffort.roundCap` with a list of all ACTIVE levers, so the new message could tell a user to raise a budget that was not the binding constraint - a property the removed code's own comment had explicitly protected. The agent chose the reviewer's first option (compute the difficulty ceiling separately and attribute) over softening the wording, which is the option that keeps the message truthful.
guidance_note: When generalizing a diagnostic from one lever to several, carry forward the property the single-lever version guaranteed - name only the constraint that actually bound - instead of only its text.

evidence: The named fix commit 92c5d02 touched src/run.js and test/difficulty-policy.test.js only, not src/difficulty-policy.js, so DIFFICULTY_BANDS and its Array.find are original PR code and the flag is a false positive. The premise holds on its own terms: find() returns the first covering band, the ascending-order requirement lived only in a comment, and the agent adopted the reviewer's own second option (a smallest-covering reduce).
guidance_note: An invariant a table's consumer depends on belongs in the selection function, not in a comment above the table.

evidence: I re-ran the agent's check independently: 50*0.4 === 20, 200*0.4 === 80 and 625*0.4 === 250 are all exact in IEEE-754, and an exhaustive scan of n in 0..5000 against exact rational comparison (2n vs 5*maxMagnitude) produced 0 mismatches, so the reviewer's specific claim that 50*0.4 evaluates to 20.000000000000004 is false. The named fix commit e0ee8cb inserted selectBand above effortMagnitude but left the multiplication untouched, so the flag is a relocation false positive.

The reduce that ties on equal maxMagnitude was introduced by e0ee8cb, the fix for F2, whose stated purpose was to make band selection order-INDEPENDENT; `b.maxMagnitude < a.maxMagnitude` is false on ties, so the property the fix claimed held only for tables with unique values. The flag names 64000ed, which touched only test/difficulty-policy.test.js, so the real cause is F2's fix one commit earlier.
guidance_note: When replacing an order-dependent selection with an order-independent one, make the comparator total - a strict `<` reduce still falls back to array order on ties, so the claimed property is false for the degenerate table.

evidence: The 92c5d02 test patch shows the exhaustiveness loop was added by F1's fix and asserts only `if (r.deRated) assert.ok(budgetBound || difficultyBound)` - the one direction the current code happens to produce - while the skip-message relies on the iff. The reviewer is right that the reverse is provable from transitivity, so this is a partially-pinned invariant rather than a live bug, and the agent's full-iff strengthening is proportionate.
guidance_note: When a consumer relies on an iff between two computed flags, assert both directions in the exhaustive loop you write for the fix, not the direction the current implementation happens to satisfy.

evidence: The repo's package.json sets "main": "dist/index.js" with no files/publish config and the package is not on the npm registry (registry.npmjs.org returns not-found), so no external consumer can require src/run.js and the runtime break the reviewer describes has no possible caller - the reviewer had already hedged this itself. The named fix commit 61d0581 touched difficulty-policy.js and its test, not budget.js, so the signature change it flags is original PR code.

narrative: Five rounds on a nine-file wiring PR, and this is the packet where fix-caused findings actually cost a round. Both round-3 findings trace to earlier fixes: F2's order-independence fix left a non-total comparator (F4), and F1's attribution fix shipped a one-directional test for an invariant the skip-message relies on (F5). Had either been complete, round 3 would have been empty and round 4 would not exist. The two pushbacks (F3's floating-point claim, F6's breaking-export claim) were both verified correct here, and F3's is a case where accepting would have added dead rounding code against a condition that provably never fires.
guidance_observations: The two rounds that produced fix-caused findings both involved a fix that CLAIMED a property (order-independence, a full iff) in its own comment or commit message without making the claim total - the claim itself is the reliable predictor of the next round's finding.

The agent's pushback on the FP claim did the right verification (an exhaustive scan through the real code path) and reported the numbers in the thread, which is what made the pushback checkable by an auditor rather than an assertion.

evidence: The table really was [1.0, 1.0, 1.3, 1.7, 2.2] under a comment asserting STRICT MONOTONICITY, and the test used >= while naming itself strict, so neither the data nor the test enforced the documented invariant. The agent fixed the data rather than weakening the comment and tightened both tests to >, which is the direction that keeps the stated theorem true.
guidance_note: When a comment asserts an invariant over a hand-tuned table, write the test that enforces that exact invariant in the same commit as the comment.

evidence: The coupling is real: REASONING_COST_MULTIPLIER is indexed by TIER_RANK[tier] with no coverage check, and an added rank would yield undefined then NaN, which never satisfies <= cap so the candidate is silently skipped rather than failing. The agent's load-time assertion catches the same desync earlier and at the definition site instead of on every call, which is strictly better than the per-call guard proposed. The named commit 30ab770 changed only the array's values, not reasoningFactor, so the flag is a false positive.
guidance_note: When two tables must cover the same index space, assert their correspondence at the definition site as you write the second one, rather than leaving the coupling implicit.

evidence: The fold is applied by chain.map so it is correct by construction, but no test exercised the second config after a failover, which is where configUsed and the attribution footer are actually read from; the reviewer called it insurance rather than a bug and that framing is accurate. The named commit 30ab770 did not touch multiscope or its test, so the flag is a false positive.
guidance_note: When a transform is applied across a failover chain, cover the element the chain falls back TO, not only the first element.

evidence: The 95972ce patch shows the assertion F2's fix added is `if (REASONING_COST_MULTIPLIER.length <= MAX_TIER_RANK)`, which is one-directional exactly as described; the reviewer correctly notes the reverse desync is harmless today and says no fix is needed, so this is a real asymmetry with no live consequence rather than a defect. Tightening to exact equality was cheap and rode along with three other fixes in the same commit, so it cost no extra round.
guidance_note: State a table-correspondence invariant as exact equality when you first write it - a one-sided bound invites the next round's question about the other direction.

evidence: The named commit 95972ce touched budget.js, multiscope.js and their tests but not difficulty-policy.js, so `selectBand(bands, magnitude, rankOf = (b) => b.roundCap)` is original PR-92 code and the flag is a false positive. The premise is nonetheless a real latent bug: the function's own comment claims axis-agnosticism while its default keys the tie-break to one axis, so any future band table passed without an explicit rankOf compares undefined against undefined and silently reverts to array order.
guidance_note: When generalizing a function to a second axis, delete the default that encodes the first axis instead of keeping it for compatibility - the default silently mis-serves every axis added later.

evidence: `TIER_RANK[b.tier] ?? -1` genuinely cannot distinguish the legitimate null no-raise band from a misspelled tier string, and both maxTier and reasoningFactor throw on unknown tiers, so this was an inconsistency inside one codebase's own vocabulary handling. The agent's named reasoningBandRank preserves null while throwing on unknown strings, which is the only split that satisfies both cases. Original PR code, untouched by the named commit.
guidance_note: A `?? default` on a vocabulary lookup swallows out-of-vocabulary keys; separate the legitimate absent value from an unknown one and fail loudly on the latter.

evidence: The implicit assumption is real - tierAt derefs selectBand's result and the table's totality rests only on its Infinity row - but the reviewer's first suggestion, `?.`, would convert a broken-table failure into a silent undefined, which is worse in a test; the agent rejected that and took the reviewer's own third option, a totality assertion. This is test-file code untouched by the named commit 95972ce, so the flag is a false positive.
guidance_note: When a data table is required to be total, assert its totality once in a test rather than letting each consumer's deref carry the assumption.

evidence: The reviewer states in its own text that this is 'NOT a violation of one-way-deps in the strict sense', and the structure it describes is a diamond in a DAG with effort.js as the single sink - there is one definition of TIER_RANK and zero re-exports. The agent's counter is the decisive one: the only consolidation available is re-exporting TIER_RANK through budget.js, which would create the duplication the finding warns about. The import line predates the named commit 4f221d7, which used TIER_RANK that was already imported.

narrative: Four rounds, eight findings, and only one genuine chain: the load-time coverage assertion that F2's fix introduced was one-directional, which F4 then asked about. Everything else the flags mark as fix-caused is original PR code re-read by a reviewer that re-reviews the full diff each round. The technical quality here is high on both sides - F5 and F6 are real latent bugs in a generalization the agent wrote, and the agent caught that the reviewer's `?.` suggestion in F7 would have introduced silent failure. The single pushback (F8) is correct and the reviewer had already conceded it was not a violation.
guidance_observations: Round 2 raised four findings, three of them on original code the reviewer had already passed in rounds 0 and 1 - the reviewer's per-round scope is unstable, so a clean earlier round is not evidence a region is clean.

In F3 the agent bundled an unrelated pre-existing fix (forwarding sleepFn to produceReview) into a review-response commit, which widens the surface each round re-reviews and is how a review-response commit becomes the next round's finding source.

evidence: The code shown puts the resolveModuleRepo await outside the try that wraps compareCommits, and resolveModuleRepo reaches discoverGithubRepo's network fetch, so a DNS failure or timeout would reject through Promise.all in run.js and abort the whole review - directly contradicting the no-throw guarantee the function's own comment states. The agent wrapped it and added a throwing-fetchImpl regression test.
guidance_note: When a function documents a no-throw contract, put every await in the function inside the guard, not only the call you had in mind when writing the comment.

evidence: MAX_COMMITS and MAX_FILES bound one module's contribution but nothing bounded the number of modules a grouped Dependabot go.mod diff can bump, and the rendered note is replicated into every worker's prompt, so the aggregate really was unbounded. The agent capped bump count at the fetch boundary and rendered the overflow as explicit skipped entries rather than dropping them.
guidance_note: When injecting generated context into a prompt, cap the item count as well as each item - per-item bounds do not bound the aggregate.

evidence: The two instruction blocks genuinely conflict: dependencyInstructionBlock names requestChange on the go.mod version line unconditionally, while the unshowable-files block tells the reviewer to use finishReview for any file whose diff was omitted, and go.mod can land in that set. The named commit 0689901 did not touch src/prompt.js, so the flag is a false positive on original PR code.
guidance_note: When adding an instruction that names a reporting channel, check the other instructions in the same prompt for a path on which that channel is unavailable.

evidence: SAFE_MODULE_PATH constrains the shape of a diff-controlled string and then that string is interpolated into `https://${modulePath}?go-get=1`, so an attacker-authored go.mod line really could drive an outbound request from the runner to an internal host - a genuine blind SSRF, correctly scoped by the reviewer as limited by the opt-in flag. The agent rejected the host-allowlist suggestion, which would have defeated vanity-import discovery, and implemented the standard DNS pre-flight private-range refusal plus an honest README note about the residual rebinding TOCTOU. The named commit 8b1b556 touched only src/prompt.js, so the flag is a false positive.
guidance_note: When untrusted content reaches a URL, validate the resolved destination, not only the string's shape - a shape allowlist is not a destination allowlist.

evidence: Go's +incompatible is build metadata on the module version and is not part of the git tag, so refFor passing v2.0.0+incompatible straight to compareCommits would 404 and report resolved:false for a repo that is perfectly reachable - a real, common version form the mapper never handled. The named commit 1fa9f3c added the SSRF guard above refFor and renumbered it without changing it, so the flag is a relocation false positive.
guidance_note: When mapping a version string to a VCS ref, enumerate every suffix form the version grammar admits - pseudo-version, prerelease, +incompatible - before writing the mapper, instead of handling the one form you started from.

evidence: GO_MOD_REQUIRE_LINE is /^[+-][ \t]+(\S+)\s+(v\d\S*)/, which matches a replace directive's left-hand side and captures the OLD version as if it were the bump target, so a PR touching a replace block would fetch the wrong version range. Original code relocated by 1fa9f3c, not fix-caused.
guidance_note: When a line regex parses one directive of a multi-directive file format, reject the other directives explicitly rather than trusting the shape not to collide.

evidence: The inconsistency is real - SAFE_MODULE_PATH's domain class omits the underscore that every following path segment's class allows - but the reviewer's motivating case is weak, since an underscored label is not a valid DNS hostname and such a module could not be resolved anyway; the reviewer concedes it is 'extremely rare'. Widening the class is harmless because underscore cannot smuggle a scheme, credentials or a different host, so accepting was cheap and defensible even though the named use case is unreachable. Original code relocated by 1fa9f3c.
guidance_note: Derive a shape gate's character classes once from the spec you are gating against, so the same class is used at every position instead of diverging between segments.

evidence: The refFor test really did cover only plain tags and one pseudo-version, so nothing exercised the +incompatible form and the F5 bug shipped through a green suite; this finding is the test-shaped twin of F5 and the agent correctly folded it into the same fix rather than treating it as separate work. Original test code relocated by 1fa9f3c's test additions.

The 0689901 patch shows `filteredFiles.find(f => f.filename === 'go.mod' && f.patch)` as an unchanged context line, so the exact-match lookup is original PR code and the flag is a false positive. The premise is sound: a nested module such as tools/go.mod is never scanned, and find would take only the first match even if several qualified.
guidance_note: When a feature keys off a conventionally-named file, decide up front whether the convention is root-only or per-directory, and match accordingly rather than defaulting to the root.

evidence: I reproduced the agent's evidence against live GitHub: repos/golang/net/compare/v0.53.0...v0.55.0 returns commits[0] dated 2026-04-10 and the last commit dated 2026-05-22, and repos/pressly/goose/compare/v3.27.1...v3.27.3 returns 2026-05-15 first and 2026-07-22 last - ascending chronological, so slice(-MAX_COMMITS) already takes the most recent commits and the reviewer's proposed slice(0, MAX_COMMITS) would have shipped exactly the bug it described. The reviewer had asserted the same wrong ordering claim once before, in the round-1 summary body.
guidance_note: Record an external API's documented result ordering in a comment at the slice that depends on it, so neither a later reader nor a reviewer re-derives it from the wrong recollection.

evidence: The README section added by this PR documents the 8-module per-PR cap but not MAX_COMMITS=30 or MAX_FILES=50, so an operator reading the docs cannot tell that a 200-commit bump surfaces only 30 commits to the reviewer. 1fa9f3c's README change added the SSRF TOCTOU note, not this section, so the flag is a false positive.
guidance_note: When documenting a feature's limits, document every cap the feature applies, not only the outermost one.

evidence: The 1fa9f3c patch shows isPublicAddress was introduced by F4's SSRF fix with the ranges 0/8, 10/8, 127/8, 169.254/16, 172.16-31 and 192.168/16, and RFC 6598's 100.64.0.0/10 is genuinely absent - a reserved range some cloud providers use internally, so the guard added one round earlier had a hole in its own range table. The flag names 1641861, which is a dist-only rebuild.
guidance_note: Build a reserved-IP-range table from the IANA special-purpose registry rather than from the ranges you remember; RFC 6598 CGNAT is the one routinely missed.

evidence: The existing render test used totalCommits 2 with 1 commit and totalFiles 1 with 1 file, so the truncation branch that emits 'most recent N shown' was never reached even though the README documents that text as a guarantee. The named commit 1641861 is a dist-only rebuild, so this is original test code, not fix-caused.
guidance_note: Choose renderer test fixtures whose counts cross each documented cap - fixtures with matching counts leave the truncation branch unexercised while the suite still reports green.

evidence: F9's fix (60d160b) replaced the exact-equality find with `f.filename === 'go.mod' || f.filename.endsWith('/go.mod')`, which newly admits vendor/github.com/.../go.mod - paths the previous exact match correctly excluded, so the broadening reintroduced a class of false positive that had not existed before the fix. The flagged commit 1641861 is only a dist rebuild.
guidance_note: When broadening an exact match to a suffix match, enumerate the path classes the new pattern newly admits (vendor/, node_modules/, third_party/) and exclude the unwanted ones in the same change.

narrative: The largest packet: five rounds, fourteen findings, one pushback that saved a shipped bug. Two genuine chains land in round 4 - the SSRF range table F4 introduced missed CGNAT (F12), and the go.mod matcher F9 broadened to suffix matching newly swallowed vendored files (F14) - both instances of a fix widening or enumerating a set incompletely. The pushback on F10 is the batch's most valuable single event: the reviewer twice asserted that GitHub's compare API returns commits newest-first, which live API calls disprove, and accepting the proposed slice(0, N) would have shown reviewers the oldest commits under a 'most recent' label. Round 4 was not fully avoidable because F13, a genuine untested-branch finding, was independent of any fix.
guidance_observations: Round 1's summary body named two blocking bugs (+incompatible and the commit slice) but the round produced only one inline thread, and neither summary-only bug was acted on - +incompatible then resurfaced as F5 two rounds later, so a bug the reviewer had already found cost two extra rounds purely because it had no thread for address-pr-reviews to walk.

F5 and F8 are the same defect delivered as a code finding and a test finding on separate threads, which doubles the thread count without adding information; the agent correctly answered them as one fix.

Every round-3 finding was on original PR code, and every round-4 finding carried a flag pointing at 1641861, a dist-only rebuild commit - the flag heuristic treats any post-review commit as a cause, so on this repo, where dist/ is rebuilt and committed, it mislabels nearly everything.
